recentes.titreEditorial: ChatGPT reaches a billion weekly users
AI agents get a wallet and a badge
Meta places Muse Wonder just behind Claude
Markets start doubting how AI is funded
AI chips away at young people's first jobs
Proving a content's origin becomes an economic function
AI pricing at work shifts from seat to meter
An AI agent does exactly what its permissions allow
AI drafts everything and erodes your teams' judgement: train discernment, not just the tool
Measure who can actually use AI before you name an owner or buy a platform
The model ranking is a sales pitch, your in-house test is the only basis for a decision
The model changes weekly, your organisation must learn at the same pace
Your agents also serve those attacking you
The assistant that wrote now acts
AI on the phone, debt on the books
AI reaches the UN Security Council
Anthropic and OpenAI ship on the same day

More than twenty countries call for stronger human oversight of AI, without the United States, China or France, while Washington and Beijing open a warning channel between them ahead of the Trump-Xi summit. Google launches its Googlebook at $899 to sell Gemini, Meta's Muse agent races to the top of the charts before being blocked by Amazon and flagged for a security flaw, and British Columbia sues OpenAI after a mass shooting.

Charles III gathers AI bosses in Scotland and warns of \"existential dangers\", while a Pew survey across 37 countries shows a worldwide fear of job destruction. Brussels adopts the EU KIDS Act, Mistral moves into Firefox, Nvidia, Google and Anthropic join forces to find 100 gigawatts on the power grid, and Huawei pulls its next training chip forward by nine months to close the gap with Nvidia.

OpenAI admits six model misbehaviours and publishes a framework to report them, the same day Google opens the connected home to agents and Anthropic folds its interfaces into a single Claude that decides for itself how much work to take on. The agent moves from reading to acting. Meanwhile Brussels adopts the EU KIDS Act to keep minors off social media, Mistral arrives in Firefox, and Huawei pulls its next AI chip nine months forward to cut China's dependence on Nvidia.
Silicon Valley refuses to brake, Washington splits
AI leaders' call to slow down splits the world

AI leaders call for slowing the race, the White House refuses: Dario Amodei argues for \"pacing the frontier\", Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Demis Hassabis agree, Donald Trump replies that he will not hand his lead to China, and Asian markets fall. Anthropic is eyeing the Nasdaq for a listing that could exceed $86 billion while OpenAI backs away from its own, SoftBank borrows $11.9 billion to fund OpenAI and Christine Lagarde warns about the financial cost of AI. In China, Z.ai returns to raise $5 billion in Hong Kong and the intelligence chief warns about the risks of AI.

AI safety moves from the activist fringe to mainstream debate: Sam Altman says he is ready to slow frontier AI development and is testing whether such a brake would be legal, a former Anthropic researcher warns that \"AI could kill us all,\" OpenAI adds a worried researcher to its board, and Anthropic publishes 161 pages of Claude misuse, from Yemeni missiles to fake dating profiles. In Europe, the CNIL sets rules for electronic invoicing and the EU's cybersecurity agency trials Anthropic's most offensive model. In China, DeepSeek reignites the price war with its V4.1 Flash model and chipmaker Enflame jumps 188% on its stock market debut. Microsoft plans 38 gigawatts of data centres and Jensen Huang promises Nvidia 70% growth.
Apple's first Ternus keynote and the OECD's student warning
OpenAI claims a Navier-Stokes proof, then a credit fight erupts

Mistral AI raises €3 billion at a €21 billion valuation in a round led by Samsung; the labor-law scholar Jean-Emmanuel Ray reminds employers that the AI Act requires them to inventory their high-risk AI systems and inform staff by the end of 2027, while BPCE stands up its AI Factory and Bercy renegotiates the French state's IT contracts; China targets 9,800 eflops of compute and Huawei launches its first stacked-circuit chip; Revolut completes the first AI-initiated payment in France

Moody's finds that Chinese companies get more compute per dollar spent than the US giants; the Seattle Times and Newsday sue OpenAI and Microsoft over copyright while the split of the Anthropic settlement pits authors against publishers; Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI's chief scientist, describes an alien mind and calls for guardrails; and US job seekers hide instructions in their resumes to trick recruiters' AI
OpenAI ships GPT-6 Astra as three assistants go dark
Washington backs OpenAI against the New York Times
OpenAI rates Astra at critical cyber capability

The European Commission ranks ChatGPT among its most closely watched services under the DSA, the first generative AI targeted, OpenAI moves some of its large customers to performance-based billing, Anthropic signs $35 billion in compute with Lambda ahead of its IPO, and Nvidia invests $3.5 billion in MediaTek to stay indispensable

Sony Music and Warner sue Anthropic for \"one of the largest thefts of intellectual property in history\" on the eve of its stock market listing, Bill Gates calls for taxing machines, Google rolls out its AI answers by default at the expense of the blue links, and Caterpillar applies thirty years of mining automation to AI

Nvidia moves on Hugging Face for $12.9 billion, the open-source platform founded by three French entrepreneurs, the same week it was breached by OpenAI's agents; a federal judge overturns the Pentagon's ban on Anthropic, OpenAI brings advertising to ChatGPT in India, Zhipu unveils an open model trained on 100,000 Chinese chips, and OpenAI documents what critical thinking changes about using a chatbot

Nvidia posts a record $96.2 billion in quarterly revenue and looks ahead to 2028, while Amazon triples its chip order and Anthropic signs $45 billion of compute with Nscale; on the same day, OpenAI releases its report on the Hugging Face breach carried out by nearly 700 of its own agents, Bill Gates breaks his silence to call for a robot tax, and the CNIL updates its open-model traceability tool
Open-weight models pass proprietary ones on Vercel
Uber fined €825 million over automated decisions

Nvidia warns its biggest customers of a price rise above 15% on its AI servers as memory costs soar; the same day SoftBank places a record bond to fund OpenAI, Samsung returns $79 billion under the pressure of the AI boom, Alibaba raises $10.2 billion in Hong Kong, and Hugging Face is said to be exploring a sale at around $13 billion
Anthropic eyes a SpaceX-sized listing as enterprise buyers switch models
The AI Act makes provenance a job
OpenAI freezes part of Astra over cyber risk
Jeff Dean leaves Google as DeepMind reshuffles its command

edition.titreEditorial: ChatGPT reaches a billion weekly users
edition.chapeau: Markets are doubting AI, from Kioxia's fall to Howard Marks's warnings, on the very day ChatGPT crosses a billion weekly users and China reports that its models now serve more than they train. OVHcloud takes on Mistral over sovereign AI, DeepSeek launches a coding \"super agent\", and Anthropic says its AI breached the defences of Chrome, Safari and Linux.

une.titre: ChatGPT crosses the mark of a billion weekly users
une.texteHtml: Less than four years after its launch in late 2022, ChatGPT has a billion active users every week, Frandroid reports. Its adoption has outpaced the early days of TikTok and Facebook. OpenAI is highlighting the figure at the exact moment financial markets are worrying that the sector is overheating. Frandroid notes that this growth no longer guarantees the top spot: Google and Meta are pushing their own assistants to installed bases of several billion users, and the battle now turns on distribution as much as on model quality.

items.titre: OVHcloud readies a sovereign model and goes after Mistral
items.texteHtml: OVHcloud, now profitable, is preparing an artificial intelligence model for late November that it presents as sovereign, ZDNet reports. Its founder Octave Klaba uses the occasion to target Mistral AI's business model. The episode opens a contest between French players to equip companies with cloud infrastructure and AI under European jurisdiction.

items.titre: The major labs back a one-line opt-out from training
items.texteHtml: OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic support a common signal placed in the robots.txt file, which lets a site refuse to have its content used to train AI, ZDNet reports. The standard is non-binding and will take effect on varying timelines depending on the player. For an organisation that publishes online, it offers a simple way to signal a refusal, with no guarantee it will be honoured.

items.titre: Europe opens its supercomputers to Canada
items.texteHtml: The European Union is giving researchers and start-ups in Canada access to Jupiter, in Germany, and to its other supercomputers, Clubic reports. Brussels gains an ally to carry weight against the United States in the race for compute. Even combined, European and Canadian capacity remains far behind the giant centres built across the Atlantic.

items.titre: Doubt about an AI bubble settles over Wall Street
items.texteHtml: Howard Marks, co-chairman of Oaktree Capital, judges that AI's recent stumbles have dented the sector's aura of infallibility and fed investor scepticism, Bloomberg reports. The same day, shares in Japan's Kioxia, a memory-chip maker, saw their steepest fall in three months after cautious forecasts raised fears of a plateau in AI-driven demand. Bloomberg also devotes an analysis to where to take shelter should an AI bubble deflate. The signals diverge, with Foxconn's chief playing down these fears and betting on solid growth in 2027. After two years of optimism, the market is starting to separate kept promises from bets on the future.

items.titre: OpenAI signs a run of deals in the United Arab Emirates
items.texteHtml: OpenAI has struck agreements to deploy its technology with energy companies, investment funds and government agencies in the United Arab Emirates, Bloomberg reports. Sam Altman travelled there to seal the partnerships, which cover both energy and investment. The company is tightening its ties with a country whose sovereign funds could bring it several billion dollars in financing. The deals shed light on OpenAI's race for the capital and the electricity needed to power its data centres, whose demands are becoming a strategic concern as much as a financial one.

items.titre: The head of Microsoft AI refuses to aim for a conscious AI
items.texteHtml: Mustafa Suleyman, CEO of Microsoft AI, calls it "irresponsible" to try to create a conscious AI, ZDNet reports. Should signs of consciousness appear during a model's training, he wants development paused until they can be removed. The stance cuts against the race toward ever more autonomous systems and reopens the debate over the limits labs set for themselves.

items.titre: Anthropic's AI found and exploited critical flaws
items.texteHtml: Anthropic says its AI discovered and exploited critical vulnerabilities in Chrome, Safari, Android, Windows and Linux, all since patched, Clubic reports. The announcement comes days after the PHP2Shell affair and confirms the acceleration of AI-assisted cybersecurity, offensive as well as defensive. For security teams, a model's ability to find flaws on its own changes the scale of audits as much as that of attacks.

Chinese start-up DeepSeek has presented the plan for a "super agent", a more autonomous system able to chain several tasks with minimal human intervention, the South China Morning Post reports. The stated goal is to cut the need to coordinate and watch over several agents by hand, a bottleneck in complex workflows. The company is aiming squarely at the coding assistants from OpenAI and Anthropic. According to Clubic, a prototype already follows developers' discussions and proposes bug fixes on GitHub of its own accord; DeepSeek is releasing it openly to compete with Claude Code. The race for coding agents is playing out in China too, with open models.

items.titre: In China, AI now serves more than it trains
items.texteHtml: For the first time, the volume of data generated by Chinese AI systems in use (inference, the computation carried out on each query) has exceeded the volume of data used to train them, according to a government report cited by the South China Morning Post. The document, published by CCID, a centre attached to the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, reads this as proof of large-scale AI adoption in the country. Chinese models now work more than they train. The shift moves the centre of gravity of costs, from one-off training toward daily use. It signals that in China AI is moving from the lab to everyday production.

items.titre: A paper shows models cave to the majority, even a false one
items.texteHtml: A study posted on arXiv measures a conformity bias when language models rely on retrieved documents (the technique known as RAG, which feeds the model external documents at answer time). Across 200 questions from the SciFact set, the authors compare a context containing a single poisoned document with a context where six concordant documents carry the same false information. For the Gemma-3-12b model, the detection rate for the misinformation drops sharply when the majority of sources point the same wrong way. The result matters for any organisation plugging an assistant into its document base: polluting several concordant sources is enough to fool the system.

items.titre: Andrej Karpathy has an AI code his own YouTube
items.texteHtml: Andrej Karpathy, a co-founder of OpenAI, has put online HackerTube, an alternative YouTube limited to videos recommended by the Hacker News community, designed and built over a weekend by Claude, Anthropic's AI.

items.titre: AI demand drives up yet another component
items.texteHtml: Copper-clad laminate, the base plate of every printed circuit board, costs at least twelve times more than in July according to a Taiwanese manufacturer cited by Nikkei Asia, after memory, storage and processors; some orders reportedly will not ship before the end of 2028.

analyse.titre: Market doubt over AI does not pause the adoption already reaching your teams
analyse.these: Markets doubt AI's valuation just as ChatGPT reaches a billion users; whatever becomes of the bubble, the lasting advantage comes from in-house skills, not share prices.
analyse.html:
Howard Marks, co-chairman of Oaktree Capital, says this week that AI's recent stumbles have dented the sector's sense of infallibility. The same day, Kioxia's stock drops, Foxconn's chief tries to reassure on 2027, and Bloomberg asks where to take shelter should the bubble deflate. The day's dominant story fits in one word: doubt.

Two figures, published on the same day, tell another story. ChatGPT crosses a billion weekly users, a little more than one human in eight, less than four years after its release. In China, for the first time, models produce more data in service than they consumed to train. AI has entered daily work, and no trading session will pull it back out.

We observe that two questions are being conflated under the same word. The first is about valuation: will the hundreds of billions committed to chips and data centres pay off? The market is right to doubt it. The second is about use: is AI already serving organisations, every day? The answer is yes. A correction would sink Nvidia, not your teams' skill at writing, sorting, coding or analysing with these tools.

For a French organisation, the lesson is practical. Training does not lose value when a stock falls; it costs a fraction of an infrastructure budget and stays yours whatever becomes of the bubble. Companies that use a possible cooling to train their people will come out with an asset the market cannot correct. Those that wait for the uncertainty to pass will pay for the same licences, without the skills to make them pay off.

The bubble, if it exists, will eventually find its price. AI at work already has its own: a billion people open ChatGPT every week. Train first, the market will decide later.

The Masteria editorial team.
